analysis.one_liner: Creates new income tax brackets up to 49% for incomes over $1 million.
analysis.headline: The bill had 11 Democratic sponsors but never received a hearing or vote, dying in the House Ways and Means Committee when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten the income tax tables so that income above $1 million is taxed at rates rising from 45% to 49%, with the top rate applied only to income above $1 billion. It would also take away the special low capital-gains rate from taxpayers whose income reaches the 45% bracket, taxing their investment gains at ordinary income rates. The bill says nothing about how the extra revenue would be used.
analysis.who_benefits: If enacted, the direct beneficiaries would be everyone outside the top bracket whose tax bill did not change, plus whatever public purposes the added revenue could serve — deficit reduction or programs — though the bill left that unspecified. The burden falls almost entirely on the roughly households and individuals reporting more than $1 million in taxable income, and hardest of all on income above $10 million.

how_it_helps.text: Adds new brackets for very high incomes: 45% on income over $1 million, 46% over $10 million, 47% over $20 million, 48% over $100 million, and 49% over $1 billion, applying only to income in each bracket above the thresholds [S3].
Leaves rates unchanged for incomes under $1 million, so no taxpayer below that threshold pays more under the bill's tables [S3].
Withdraws the preferential capital-gains rate from taxpayers whose income reaches the 45% bracket, so their investment gains are taxed like wages [S3].
Adjusts the new brackets for inflation after 2015 so they do not quietly erode over time [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers with more than $1 million in taxable income, with the cost rising steeply for the very largest incomes, and especially holders of large realized capital gains who would lose the preferential investment rate.

drawbacks.text: The bill raises revenue but never says what the money is for, so its concrete benefit to ordinary people depends entirely on decisions made elsewhere [S3].

A common objection to pushing top federal rates toward 50% — on top of state taxes — is that it widens the payoff from avoidance, deferral, and moving income out of the personal income tax, which can shrink the revenue actually collected. The bill text and summary do not address this [S3].

Taxing capital gains at ordinary rates for the highest earners reverses a long-standing preference; critics argue investment income already bears corporate tax and that higher rates on gains reduce risk-taking and lock in assets. Supporters reply that the preferential rate is the main reason the very rich pay lower effective rates than many workers [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The tradeoff is straightforward: a meaningful tax increase confined to the top few tenths of a percent of filers, in exchange for revenue whose use is left open. The design is clean on who pays, but the benefit side is indirect — the bill is a revenue raiser, not a program. The efficiency objections are real but standard for any steeply progressive rate schedule.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and never moved again; no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jan Schakowsky introduced the bill on January 14, 2015, with nine Democratic colleagues joining as original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day [S3] [S5].
The action history shows exactly two actions — introduction and the committee referral — with nothing further in the 114th Congress [S5].
Ways and Means never took the bill up, so it never reached the House floor and received no vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-income households and large investors kept the existing top rates, including the preferential capital-gains rate, because the bill never advanced. No one else's taxes changed either, so the direct effect of the outcome is that the tax code stayed as it was.

for.name: Rep. Jan Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Fairness in Taxation Act of 2015 and referred it to Ways and Means.

for.name: 9 of 188 House Democrats
for.role: Original cosponsors (Conyers, Cummings, Ellison, Grijalva, Gutiérrez, Lee, McDermott, Nadler, Norton)
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day of introduction and never held a hearing or markup on it.

against.name: Rep. Kevin Brady
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee holding the bill, never scheduled it for consideration during the 114th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 11 sponsors were House Democrats and no Republican signed on; the Republican-controlled committee never moved the bill, so it died without any vote to measure broader support.

industries.industry: Households with over $1 million in taxable income
industries.note: The bill would have raised their marginal rates to 45–49% on income above $1 million. Their stake in the bill not advancing was keeping the existing lower top rates.

industries.industry: Large investors and investment fund managers
industries.note: Anyone whose income reached the 45% bracket would have lost the preferential capital-gains rate, which is a major driver of the low effective tax rates on the wealthiest filers.

industries.industry: Tax preparation, tax planning, and wealth advisory services
industries.note: New high brackets and a capital-gains recapture rule create planning complexity that such firms both help clients manage and profit from. The bill's fate did not change their business.
